schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT AS Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X, DEPT AS Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT AS Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X, DEPT AS Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPT, LOC, MGR) VALUES (1, 3, 101); INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPT, LOC, MGR) VALUES (2, 4, 102); INSERT INTO EMP (NAME, DEPT, EMP) VALUES (101, 1, 101); INSERT INTO EMP (NAME, DEPT, EMP) VALUES (102, 2, 103);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 uses a subquery to find the manager of a department located at location 3, while Q2 directly joins the EMP and DEPT tables to find employees who are managers of departments located at location 3. The conditions in the WHERE clauses are different, leading to potentially different results.
counterexample_dsp: The difference is triggered when there is an employee who is not a manager of any department located at location 3, but is a manager of another department.
